sectionsContent.title: Molecular Polarity

concept.summary: ΔEN = higher EN − lower EN. Under 0.40: nonpolar. 0.40 to 1.80: polar. Over 1.80: ionic.
keyIdeas: Symmetric: same outer atoms, spread evenly. Polar bonds in a symmetric shape cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.
Asymmetric: different outer atoms, or lone pairs on the central atom. The pulls don't cancel, so the molecule is polar.

sectionsContent.directions: For each molecule, name the shape and draw it. Draw a dipole arrow beside each polar bond, pointing toward the δ− atom, with the cross at the δ+ end. Find ΔEN for each bond listed and show the subtraction, then mark it PC or NPC. Then decide whether the whole molecule is polar or nonpolar. We will do number 1 together.
keyNotes: Number 1 (CO₂) is done with the class (slide 23): blank on the student copy, not scored. 10 points: rows 2–11, 1 per molecule.
EN values (Pauling, as on the slides): H 2.20, B 2.04, C 2.55, N 3.04, O 3.44, P 2.19, S 2.58, Cl 3.16.

Drawings follow slides 24–30: outer lone pairs may be left off. Each polar bond gets an arrow toward δ− (cross at δ+, slide 10); a nonpolar bond (C–H, 0.35) gets none. Polar molecule: a long net arrow. Nonpolar: net = 0. Accept any clear placement pointing the right way.
CCl₄ vs CHCl₃: same shape, but in CHCl₃ the C–H pull is weaker, so the pulls do not cancel. Rows 6 and 11 need both bond lines for the point.
BCl₃: B has only 6 electrons, like BF₃ on slide 24. SO₂ is bent from the lone pair on S, so unlike CO₂ it is polar.
PCl₅ vs PCl₃: same bond (0.97). PCl₅'s pulls cancel; PCl₃'s lone pair makes a pyramid, so it is polar. HCN is linear but its ends differ: polar.
If a student asks: H₂S (0.38) and PH₃ (0.01) are slightly polar in real life because of the lone pair. The cutoffs are guidelines (slide 11).
